question: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 40^\circ$, $a = 5$ cm, and $b = 7$ cm. Use the sine formula to determine all possible values of $B$, correct to 3 significant figures, and explain why two solutions exist.
referenceAnswer: Using the sine formula: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{\sin 40^\circ} = \frac{7}{\sin B}$, so $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{5} \approx 0.900$. Thus $B \approx 64.1^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 64.1^\circ = 116^\circ$. Two solutions exist because $\sin B$ is positive in both first and second quadrants, and $b > a > b \sin A$, satisfying the ambiguous case (Case 3).
evidence: ‘$\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{5}$, $B = 64.145^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 64.145^\circ$, $\therefore B = 64.1^\circ$ or $116^\circ$, cor. to 3 sig. fig.’ — an example of Case 3

question: Given $\triangle ABC$ with $A = 120^\circ$, $b = 9$ cm, and $a = 5\sqrt{3}$ cm, show that no triangle can be formed. Justify your conclusion using angle sum and the sine formula.
referenceAnswer: By the sine formula: $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A} \Rightarrow \sin B = \frac{b \sin A}{a} = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{5\sqrt{3}}$. Since $\sin 120^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, this simplifies to $\sin B = \frac{9 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{5\sqrt{3}} = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9$, so $B \approx 64.2^\circ$. Then $A + B \approx 120^\circ + 64.2^\circ = 184.2^\circ > 180^\circ$, violating the triangle angle sum property. Hence, no triangle exists.
evidence: ‘$\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{5\sqrt{3}}$, $B = 64.158^\circ$, $A + B = 120^\circ + 64.158^\circ = 184.158^\circ > 180^\circ$, i.e. $\triangle ABC$ cannot be formed.’
subject: math

question: In $\triangle ABC$, $B = 30^\circ$ and $AB = 20$ cm. Explain why the minimum possible length of $AC$ is $10$ cm, and state the geometric configuration that achieves this minimum.
referenceAnswer: The length $AC$ is minimized when $AC \perp BC$, i.e., when $AC$ is the perpendicular from $A$ to line $BC$. In this right triangle, $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{AC}{20}$, so $AC = 20 \sin 30^\circ = 20 \times \frac{1}{2} = 10$ cm. This is the shortest possible distance from $A$ to line $BC$.
evidence: ‘When $AC \perp BC$, the length of $AC$ is minimum and $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{AC}{20 \text{ cm}}$, $AC = 20 \sin 30^\circ \text{ cm} = 10 \text{ cm}$’
subject: math

question: For $\triangle ABC$ with $B = 30^\circ$ and $AB = 20$ cm, determine the range of $AC$ for which exactly two distinct triangles can be formed. Justify your answer using the ambiguous case conditions.
referenceAnswer: Two triangles can be formed when $AC$ satisfies $b \sin B < AC < b$, where $b = AB = 20$ cm and $B = 30^\circ$. So $20 \sin 30^\circ < AC < 20$, i.e., $10 \text{ cm} < AC < 20 \text{ cm}$. This is the condition for the ambiguous case (Case 2), where side $AC$ (opposite $B$) is longer than the altitude but shorter than the adjacent side $AB$.
evidence: ‘When two triangles can be formed, $10 \text{ cm} < AC < AB$, $10 \text{ cm} < AC < 20 \text{ cm}$’
subject: math

question: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 40^\circ$, $b = 7$ cm, and $a = 10$ cm. Find $B$, correct to 3 significant figures, and explain why only one solution exists.
referenceAnswer: By the sine formula: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} \Rightarrow \sin B = \frac{b \sin A}{a} = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{10} \approx 0.450$, so $B \approx 26.7^\circ$. Only one solution exists because $a > b$, meaning side $a$ is opposite the given angle $A$ and is longer than side $b$, so $B$ must be acute (Case 4). The obtuse angle $180^\circ - 26.7^\circ = 153^\circ$ would make $A + B > 180^\circ$, which is impossible.
evidence: ‘$\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{10}$, $B = 26.7^\circ$, cor. to 3 sig. fig.’ — an example of Case 4
